claims.detail: TypeSafe AI introduced Jev as its first model aimed at software decision-making rather than human conversation. The system is designed to classify, score, route and verify information, returning machine-readable results that applications can use directly. TypeSafe calls it a “System One Model,” drawing on the distinction between fast, intuitive judgments and slower deliberate reasoning. Its stated purpose is to handle repeated small decisions inside automated workflows while leaving complex explanations to conventional language models.

Jev accepts unstructured program state and typed questions, then returns probabilistic decisions in one parallel pass instead of generating text token by token. Its documented decision primitives include categorical Choice, numeric or rubric-based Score, and a binary probability operation. The output schema is defined in advance, so the application receives typed values without parsing a generated paragraph. This design is intended for bounded answer spaces and is not suitable for open-ended writing, code generation or tasks requiring a written rationale.

TypeSafe describes Jev’s training approach as Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions, or RLCD. The stated objective is to produce probabilities that are epistemically honest on System One tasks rather than optimizing for human-rated text preferences or rubric-based textual answers. The interview characterizes Jev as a machine-native model in which software, rather than a person, consumes the output. However, the RLCD method is described as novel and unpublished, so its reward function and implementation cannot yet be independently assessed.

TypeSafe reports Jev response times between 70 and 500 milliseconds for suitable tasks and presents it as faster than conventional language models. The company lists input pricing at $0.042 per million tokens, with the model available through a hosted API. Heise notes that the speed comparisons and evaluations come from TypeSafe itself rather than an independent test. The article also says Jev became available in early access in September 2026, after TypeSafe emerged from stealth and announced $40 million in seed funding.
claims.conflicts_with: https://www.the-independent.com/tech/jev-ai-artificial-intelligence-explained-b3054446.html reports a broader claim that Jev is nearly 200 times faster and 450 times cheaper than ChatGPT and Claude, while the Heise source gives a 70–500 millisecond range without establishing that universal multiplier.

claims.detail: The Independent reports TypeSafe’s claim that Jev is almost 200 times faster and 450 times cheaper than competing systems such as ChatGPT and Claude. The model achieves this by producing constrained decisions and confidence values rather than conversational text. The article gives an example in which Jev reads an email and returns a yes-or-no judgment with an associated level of certainty. It also records TypeSafe’s claim that the restricted output format prevents hallucinations, while noting that conventional language models remain useful for chat, coding agents and other tasks requiring generated text.
claims.conflicts_with: https://www.kingy.ai/blog/typesafe-jev-review-the-ai-model-that-doesnt-generate-text states that Jev’s type constraints prevent malformed or undeclared outputs but do not prevent semantically wrong decisions, making the broader “cannot hallucinate” claim narrower than the Independent’s presentation.

claims.detail: Kingy reports that TypeSafe evaluated Jev across 711 cases covering security incidents, agent-trace observability, invoice processing and customer service. Jev’s reported scores were 61.7%, 71.6%, 61.8% and 76.0% respectively, for an aggregate of 67.8% at an estimated $0.0004 and 0.4 seconds per case. The reference answers were built from the average judgments of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 rather than independently verified operational ground truth. The review therefore treats the results as useful workflow comparisons but not definitive evidence of correctness or general intelligence.

Anthony Maio reports that Jev averaged 67.8% agreement with TypeSafe’s reference answers across four internal workflows, compared with 67.9% for GPT Terra, 74.1% for GPT Sol and 73.1% for Claude Opus 5. Jev’s reported cost and latency were $0.0004 and 0.4 seconds per case, while the Terra comparison was listed at $0.0304 and 10.1 seconds. Invoice processing showed a particularly wide gap, with Jev at 61.8% against Sol at 79.1%. The analysis emphasizes that the labels came from other models and that the test did not establish calibration, general intelligence or production reliability.

Jev is presented as a decision layer that returns probabilities, choices and scores while ordinary application code retains control of thresholds, permissions, branching and side effects. Kingy reports a TypeSafe cookbook test in which 13 questions against one shared document were handled in a batch that was 11.5 times cheaper and 9.6 times faster than 13 sequential calls. This benefit reflects shared-state batching rather than a universal speed advantage over every language model. The integration burden shifts toward defining labels, setting confidence thresholds, handling uncertain cases and evaluating errors on the customer’s own data.

DataCamp describes Jev as appropriate for high-volume, repeated decisions where the possible answers are known before the request is made. Suggested applications include support-ticket routing, classification, scoring, security checks, agent workflows and applying a decision across large datasets. The model can return calibrated probabilities so developers can automatically act above a threshold and send uncertain cases to a human or a slower language model. It is explicitly characterized as unsuitable for chat, code generation and tasks that require natural-language explanation.

Outcome School explains that Jev restricts answers to declared options, fixed score ranges or binary outcomes and attaches a probability to each result. This schema prevents an invalid label or malformed type from being returned, which reduces a class of parser and integration failures. The same source cautions that Jev can still select the wrong permitted answer, so type safety does not guarantee semantic correctness. It places Jev in routing, guardrail, scoring and real-time decision roles rather than writing, open-ended reasoning, image or audio generation.
claims.conflicts_with: https://www.the-independent.com/tech/jev-ai-artificial-intelligence-explained-b3054446.html reports TypeSafe’s broader claim that Jev is inherently unable to hallucinate, whereas Outcome School limits that claim to schema and type constraints and expressly says the model can still be wrong.

claims.detail: Heise identifies TypeSafe AI as a startup co-founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida and says Jev was released for machine-to-machine decision-making. The company was founded in 2024 and emerged from stealth in September 2026 after roughly two years of development. TypeSafe also announced $40 million in seed financing at the launch. Jev was offered through an early-access hosted API, with the company positioning it for routing, tool selection and security checks as well as general structured decisions.
